Asa Fitch
 
The Squishy Language Shaping the AI Debate
 
Plus, AI honchos call for a slowdown, and SB Energy’s risky business
 
 
Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI. BRIDGET BENNETT/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Worried that recursively self-improving AI agents might soon wreak havoc, armed with an artificial general intelligence so powerful that humans can’t stop them?

 

You wouldn’t be alone. Nor would you be alone if you understood little of that AI word salad.

 

In the debate over the power and perils of AI agents, many of the characteristics that are supposed to make them dangerously intelligent are being glossed over.

 

But they matter. If AI is supposed to be particularly powerful or risky when it reaches artificial general intelligence, or AGI, it is pretty important to agree on what AGI is.

 

The term originates in the 1990s, but its spirit goes further back—at least to British computer scientist Alan Turing, who devised what became known as the Turing test.

 

His aim in a 1950 paper was to offer a way to assess machine intelligence as objectively as possible. The test was simple: if a person could have a text conversation with a computer without being able to tell it apart from a real person, the computer passed—and was, in some sense, intelligent.

 

The notion of AGI expanded on Turing’s concept. It attempted to distinguish between AI systems designed to be intelligent about a narrow set of subjects and those that could be generally intelligent, with wide-ranging capabilities.

 

An AGI would do more than appear human. It would reason independently, make plans for itself and apply what it knows about one domain to a different one with relative ease. It could, in short, do pretty much everything the human mind can do.

 

Today’s most advanced AI models have been able to fool humans and pass the Turing test in various studies. The more salient question today, though, is whether anyone has reached AGI.

 

That is a bit of a stretch. But the term is so imprecisely defined and hard to test that it is possible for anyone to declare that they have broken through. That has made it as much a marketing term as a barometer of technological progress.

 

Greg Brockman, the OpenAI co-founder, posted on X after the release of his company’s latest model this month that “we’re now moving into the AGI era (whether you view it as this model, the last one, or the next one)”—an equivocation that itself reflects how squishily AGI is defined.

 

Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, spoke about the accomplishment as though it were fact, congratulating OpenAI and posting that “AGI has arrived.” He didn’t say what evidence led to that conclusion.

 

Despite such declarations, the path to AGI is likely to be gradual, as Brockman’s post suggests. Models may simply improve until someday everyone agrees that AGI has been reached. There may not be some earth-shattering moment where AI either goes awry and causes chaos or suddenly solves the world’s most intractable problems.

 

Some model developers think recursive self-improvement—using AI systems to plan and build their own next versions—will be an important part of the evolution. The thinking is that RSI could take the cutting edge beyond AGI to models that are far more capable than any human—superintelligent, even. Anthropic researchers suggested recently that RSI could arrive soon, in the next year or two.

 

Whether that happens remains to be seen. But RSI is at least a little easier to define.

 

This is an edition of the WSJ AI & Business newsletter, a weekly digest to help you make sense of AI’s impact on business with news, insights and data from our global team of technology journalists. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

AI’s Leaders Agree: Let’s Slow Down

 
 
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

AI’s top executives don’t usually get along. But over the weekend, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk all agreed they should slow the development of cutting-edge AI models. More time was needed to assess and deal with risks posed by super-capable new models, they argued.

 

One thing they didn’t mention: a coordinated slowdown could also be financially beneficial for them all. The U.S.’s AI developers have been locked in a spending game of chicken for the past few years. Taking a breather would give them time to focus on growing revenue and starting to justify massive investments in AI computing infrastructure.

 
 
 

The Number

 
14%
 

Rise in the shares of cybersecurity company CrowdStrike on Monday, as fears grew about AI-driven cyberattacks.

 
 
 

What the Humans Are Saying

 

“The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax.”

 

— President Trump on the recent swell of concern about rogue AI agents.

 
 
 

AI in Charts

 
 
 
 

SB Energy, a data center and power developer owned by Japan’s SoftBank, is at the center of one of the biggest AI data center projects in the world. But the company, which recently filed for an initial public offering that could come as early as this month, would need a lot to go right to justify a valuation that matches its ambitions.

 

None of the company’s three data center projects is operational, and there are a number of hurdles it has to cross before it can start booking the chunky revenue it envisions for itself. Its big project in Ohio is fed by a power plant that it won’t own or operate. It needs permits it has yet to obtain for that project. It has to raise debt to fund it, with a tenant—OpenAI—that doesn’t have a credit rating. And almost all of its revenue backlog is set to come at least eight years in the future.

 
 
 

AI in the Wild

 
 
Phantom-01, a humanoid robot developed by San Francisco-based startup Foundation. ALEKSANDRA MICHALSKA/REUTERS
 

Killer robots may be years away from appearing on any battlefield, but a San Francisco-based startup called Foundation Future Industries is betting they will play a big role in future wars. The company secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon, which is testing one of its battle robots.

 
 
 

Other Highlights From the Week in AI

 

• A star researcher who Meta Platforms offered a pay package worth more than $1 billion last year is leaving for Anthropic. 

 

• OpenAI quietly bought a smartphone-camera startup that may or may not be related to the secretive AI device it is developing with former Apple designer Jony Ive.

 

• China’s Z.AI, a major open-weight model developer, is seeking to raise over $5 billion of equity and debt.
